newsitem.title: USA: How the inflation factor affects paychecks.
newsitem.headline: How the inflation factor affects paychecks.

text.p: A battle over tiny percentages and the placement of decimal points is being fought in Washington, and the outcome will affect peoples' pocketbooks both as wage-earners and taxpayers.
At issue is the seemingly mundane subject of how the Bureau of Labour Statistics calculates the economy's inflation rate.
If the Bureau of Labour Statistics is overstating the inflation rate of the consumer price index and adjusts it lower, repercussions could include:
-- Millions of workers whose contracts include cost-of-living hikes tied to CPI will automatically get smaller raises.
-- Employers who use the CPI as a benchmark to justify their annual pay increases are likely to offer workers less.
-- Social Security recipients will receive checks with fewer cost-of-living adjustment dollars.
-- Tax rebates given to low-income workers entitled to the Earned Income Tax Credit will drop.
-- And income taxes will go up if the tax bracket cutoffs that affect taxpayers' exemptions are not as high.

Those who believe the CPI's inflation rate should be lowered argue it will be a tonic for the economy, strengthen the financial underpinnings of the Social Security system, narrow the federal budget deficit and cut income tax bills.
It would also ease the pension burdens on municipal and state governments and would leave employers with more cash on hand.
The Senate named a commission to study the matter, headed by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin. Boskin earlier headed the Council of Economic Advisers under President Bush.
When the Boskin Commission reported back last December, it told the Senate the actual inflation rate was 1.1 percentage points under the CPI figure of 2.9 percent (1995-96 period).
Fiddling with economic figures doesn't go over well in every segment.

"If you're telling firms that the CPI overstates inflation, you're giving them an absolute green light to lower the increase they give their workers," said Tom Palley, chief economist for the AFL-CIO.

In an article appearing in the April issue of The Atlantic, Palley accused the Boskin Commission of "cooking the books," a charge Harvard economist and commission member Dale Jorgenson termed "irresponsible."

The Boskin Commission's findings, Jorgenson alleged, are under attack from groups with a vested interest in high cost-of-living allowances. Such groups, he said, include the AFL-CIO, the American Association of Retired Persons, and advocates of fatter military and civil service pensions.

Jorgenson acknowledged there would be fewer benefits if the CPI inflation rate is revised downward, but "those benefits are all bought and paid for by the American taxpayer. We're talking big bucks here."
If the CPI inflation rate is lowered, Jorgenson said, "all kinds of wonderful things will happen," including a reduction in the budget deficit by $1 trillion over the next 12 years.
What's more, he said, "tax rates will actually go down over time as the federal deficit is cut, and the Social Security system will be viable instead of going broke."
To its credit, Jorgenson said, the Bureau of Labour Statistics has recognised that it overstated inflation and "has been moving in the right direction to rectify the problem."

The lower rate of inflation in the first half of this year of just 2.2 percent, as compared with 1995-96, he said, is due in part to the Bureau of Labour Statistics' actions to make the CPI more accurate.

Former Bureau of Labour Statistics head Janet Norwood, now a senior fellow at the Urban Institute in Washington, said the Boskin Commission offered no research to back up much of its criticism and expressed hope that any changes by Congress "are on hold" as the Bureau of Labour Statistics "has under way a series of normal modernisations" of the CPI.

Such changes are technical in nature and beyond the scope of this column. But as far as predicted outcomes are concerned if the inflation factor is lowered, both sides have a point. The immediate impact on workers' paychecks, Social Security recipients and taxpayers could be negative. But the longer-term impact on the economy could be positive.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a free-lance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
